citation.title: The Effect of Images of Michelle Obama's Face on Trick-or-Treaters' Dietary Choices: A Randomized Control Trial

standing_assumptions:
The paper is a six-page empirical report with no theorem, no displayed formula and no formal model; it states no potential-outcome notation and no identification assumption. The setting, as printed (read from the page images):
Abstract, Design (p. 1/6): "Multi-year randomized control trial." Intervention (p. 1/6): "Random assignment to the Michelle Obama side of the porch or the Comparison side of the porch." Main outcome measure (p. 1/6): "Selection of fruit over candy." Methods (p. 1/6): "Difference-in-means estimates."
Methods (pp. 2/6-3/6): "We ran the following versions of an experiment during Halloween trick-or-treating in 2012 (n = 165, on average 7.8 years old and 58% male), 2014 (n = 422, on average 8.5 years old and 56% male), and 2015 (n = 636, on average 8.7 years old and 49% male): children were randomly assigned to one of two sides of a porch (In 2012, random assignment was done via drawing pieces of paper from a brown bag; In 2014 and 2015 random assignment was a pseudo-random process via queuing order of children and the speed with which each side completed the last participant)."
Methods (p. 3/6): "One side of the porch–denoted Obama–had a large photo of Michelle Obama in front of the children. The other side–denoted Comparison–had a photo of Ann Romney (2012), a photo of Hillary Clinton (2014, 2015), or no photo (2014, 2015). (See S1 Table for the disaggregation of comparison groups.) Other posters were taped to the wall that said either “Obama” or “Romney”/“Clinton” on the respective sides of the porch. In 2014, we primed the trick-or-treater by pointing to the photo and asking if they knew who that was; in 2015, trick-or-treaters were individually randomly assigned (using a pre-coded Excel spreadsheet) to receive or not receive the additional priming. We pool our analysis, irrespective of this additional source of variation."
Outcome (p. 3/6): "At both sides of the porch, children were asked their age and whether they would prefer to receive fruit (a box of raisins) or candy (a more typical small packaged piece of name-brand chocolate such as Snickers or Milky Ways). Each child was given the option (fruit or candy) that they requested."
Analysis (pp. 3/6-4/6): "For analysis, we use the difference-in-means estimates for each year. (We had missing outcome data on one 12 year old, female participant in 2012; this participant is dropped from analysis. Our findings are substantively unchanged by imputing either a fruit or candy outcome for the participant.) To compute the pooled estimates, we aggregate across years using inverse probability of treatment weighting. For all estimates, we form Wald-type confidence intervals using a normal approximation-based estimation using heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors as calculated in R 3.2.3."
Not varied or measured in the study: exposure to the Let’s Move initiative, or any link between the porch condition and the initiative's health message (Introduction, p. 2/6: "an experimental evaluation of the effects of the entire campaign would not be possible due to the initiative being rolled out across the United States through mass media"). The targets below exist only because finding P035-E001 is rated Major and its validators gave an exact finite counterexample; none of the paper's headline claims is a mathematical statement.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Abstract, Conclusions (first sentence), with Abstract, Results
canonical_claim.location: Abstract Conclusions/Results, p. 2/6 (PDF p. 2), and campaign-effect wording in Results and conclusions, p. 5/6 (PDF p. 5); read with the Introduction's contextual hypothesis and rationale
canonical_claim.statement:
Abstract, Conclusions (p. 2/6): "Michelle Obama’s initiative to reduce childhood obesity has influenced children’s dietary preferences. Whether this influence extends beyond Halloween trick-or-treating in New Haven, CT on the porch of an economics professor requires further research."
The evidence it rests on, Abstract, Results (p. 2/6): "We estimate that viewing a photograph of Michelle Obama’s face relative to control conditions caused children to be 19% more likely to choose fruit over candy."
Contextual hypothesis and rationale, not a separate categorical attribution. Introduction (p. 2/6): "However, we have experimentally assessed the microfoundations of Let’s Move in order to evaluate whether the public health campaign altered dietary decision-making. When children are exposed to the image of a figurehead regularly associated with the public health campaign’s message, the subconscious reminder may reinforce the message." 
The separate campaign-effect wording. Results and conclusions (p. 5/6): "In particular, this is a strongly Democratic neighborhood, and if children in Democratic households are either more aware of Michelle Obama’s campaign or more favorably disposed to it, we would generate an overestimate of the treatment effect of her campaign on the general population of those in the United States."
Qualification the paper attaches (Introduction, p. 2/6): "While the campaign gained publicity, an experimental evaluation of the effects of the entire campaign would not be possible due to the initiative being rolled out across the United States through mass media."
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: "Michelle Obama’s initiative": the Let’s Move Initiative (Introduction, p. 2/6: "In 2010, Obama unveiled her Let’s Move Initiative, aimed at fostering a healthy lifestyle and reducing childhood obesity."). "Dietary preferences": observed as the choice of fruit (a box of raisins) or candy (Methods, p. 3/6). The Obama and Comparison conditions (Methods, p. 3/6). The pooled estimates (Results and conclusions, pp. 4/6-5/6): "28.1% (95% CI 23.8–32.4%) of participants in the Obama treatment select fruit instead of candy, in contrast to only 23.5% (20.5–26.5%) of participants in the pooled comparison group. The difference is statistically significant at the 0.10 level (two-sided p = 0.091)." The paper defines neither "influenced" nor any assumption linking the porch condition to the initiative.
canonical_claim.note:
Not a mathematical statement: an empirical causal attribution with no formal hypotheses, listed because finding P035-E001 (Major) touches it and the brief asks for the statement as printed. Its only formalizable content is the inference it draws, namely that every potential-outcome model consistent with the design (randomized porch assignment, consistency, no interference) and with the observed arm frequencies has a nonzero effect of the initiative. That rendering is this audit's reading for the purpose of the counterexample, not the paper's wording, and P035-T1 refutes it. Lean cannot decide whether the initiative in fact influenced these children. If nothing can be stated beyond the universal claim that P035-T1 already refutes, not_applicable is the right status. The brief's priority scale has no level for a printed statement that is not a mathematical headline result; 3 is used so that it comes after the counterexample and the corrected statement.

Accepted review: the categorical attribution under scrutiny is the abstract conclusion and the campaign-effect wording on p. 5/6. The Introduction explicitly discloses the implemented porch intervention, says that evaluation of the entire nationwide campaign is impossible, and offers campaign reinforcement as something that may occur. Its purpose and may-reinforce rationale are context, not separate categorical errors or required corrections. That rationale imposes neither an exclusion nor a bound on non-campaign pathways. The two exact observationally equivalent worlds establish nonidentification without refuting reinforcement as a possible explanation, deciding the real-world campaign effect, or altering the numerical porch-condition evidence. The Major finding is retained on this narrower basis.
